# Brand Repositioning — Continuity of Intent, Novelty of Expression
## Recommendation for the Sponsor Group

**Version 1.0 — complete. Prepared for sponsor-group decision, and for prior circulation to the brand team, the top four retail account leads, and Legal/Regulatory. Not yet for trade or consumer communication, and specifically not yet for agency briefing.**

---

### How we would ask you to use this

One note, then the substance.

This paper does not contain a campaign. It contains an argument about *sequence*, and a small number of decisions with money and a date attached (§10). Our reading of the two previous modernisation attempts is that neither failed on craft — both were, by the usual measures, competent work. They failed on **order of operations**: the brand asked to be seen differently before it had given anyone new a reason to look, and it did so in a register the loyal base experienced as a public disavowal of themselves. That is a sequencing failure, and sequencing failures are the cheapest kind to avoid and the most expensive kind to repeat.

Two courtesies we would ask before this travels further.

First, that the **loyal base hears about any visible change from us, in our own channels, before it encounters that change in culture or on shelf**. The likeliest single cause of avoidable damage is a 68-year-old customer of thirty years learning that "their" brand has been reinvented from a screenshot of an ad mocking the version they loved. We would rather over-invest in that courtesy than defend the alternative.

Second, that the **top four retail accounts see §§4 and 7 before the trade press sees anything at all**. A repositioning that a buyer first hears about from a journalist has already forfeited the shelf argument it depends on.

The cohort cards in §6 are **working hypotheses, offered so that they can be corrected**. Where the brand team or an account holds better data, that data replaces the card and the card is retired. A card returned unamended will be read not as agreement but as a sign that the conversation has not yet happened.

---

## 1. Recommendation on a page

**Reposition on continuity of intent, not on youth. Fix a very small brand core as inviolable; make everything else freely renewable. Earn relevance through proof — product, format, occasion, availability — before claiming it in communication. Never subtract in public. Run a protected base-reassurance track in parallel from day one, and gate each phase on base health rather than on internal enthusiasm.**

| | |
|---|---|
| The positioning line (internal, not a tagline) | **"The standard we set 70 years ago, in the form the next 70 years need."** Heritage reframed from nostalgia to *evidence of a standard* — proof of consistency, not an invitation to remember |
| What is fixed | **Four brand invariants only** (§3) — the core promise, the two or three genuinely distinctive assets, the quality proof, and the tone floor. Each stated as a floor, each with a named-approver alternative-form route (§3.6) |
| What is free | Format, occasion, price architecture, sub-brand naming, channel, casting, register, collaboration partners, packaging craft, pace |
| Year 1 shape | **Four instrumented probes** — one new format/occasion, one channel-native entrant line, one craft-transparency content stream, one base-reassurance programme — deliberately different in design, identical in instrumentation (§7) |
| What we would not do in Year 1 | A master-brand relaunch film. A new logo. A tagline change. A "we've changed" announcement in any form |
| Principal risk | **Not youth indifference — base defection and retailer nervousness.** Under-35 recruitment is slow and recoverable; base trust is fast to lose and effectively non-recoverable (§8) |
| The mockery test | Every asset passes a pre-mortem panel: *if this were screenshotted with a hostile caption, is the caption already written?* If yes, it does not ship (§5.4) |
| Measurement | 25–34 **household penetration and repeat**, weighted 60%; unaided distinctive-asset attribution 20%; earned/organic mention quality 20%. Awareness and "brand consideration" are explicitly *not* success measures — the brand has awareness and it has not helped |
| Numeric failure test | Under-35 aided consideration up ≥5 pts while 25–34 penetration flat (<0.5 pt) and base 12-month repeat down >2 pts = declared failure, programme paused at that phase gate, no further capital (§8.5) |
| Investment sought | **$14.6M Year 1, $19.2M Year 2** (illustrative; assumptions at §10.1), of which **$10.4M is reallocation** from existing A&P and only **$4.2M is incremental** in Year 1 |
| Decisions requested | **Three** — §10.4, sought at the sponsor group meeting on **18 March** |
| Owner | A small, named, cross-functional squad with delegated authority to ship inside agreed guardrails, reporting to the sponsor group and not through the existing brand-approval chain (§9.2) |

### 1.1 The core proposition, and how confident we are in it

**Younger consumers do not reject old brands. They reject brands that perform youth.** Age is not the liability; *pretending* is. A 70-year-old brand has access to a claim that no new entrant can buy — that it has been doing this, the same way, for seventy years, and can show you — and the previous campaigns traded that asset away in exchange for borrowed contemporary signalling that the brand had not earned and could not sustain.

*This is our considered practitioner assertion, not a finding (see evidence key, §12). We flag it because the sponsor group is entitled to know which of our statements are evidenced and which are judgement.*

---

## 2. Diagnosis before we design

### 2.1 The framing we would gently ask the sponsor group to test

The problem is currently described as a brand-perception problem. The available evidence may instead describe a **format, occasion and availability** problem wearing brand-perception clothing. Only one of those responds to repositioning work, and we would rather know which we have before committing eight figures to the wrong one.

| Candidate driver of under-35 decline | What a repositioning campaign does to it |
|---|---|
| The product is right but the **format/pack size** does not fit under-35 households, spaces or occasions | Nothing — needs range work |
| The brand is absent from the **channels where the cohort actually shops** (marketplace, quick-commerce, discovery-led retail) | Nothing — needs distribution work; awareness without availability is a tax |
| **Price-per-unit architecture** blocks trial at the entry point | Nothing — the entry price wins every time |
| The **occasion the brand serves has itself declined**, independent of brand age | Actively harmful — repositions into a shrinking room |
| The cohort has **no problem with the brand and no reason to think about it** | Improves, *if* paired with proof and availability |
| The cohort **actively codes the brand as their parents'** and that coding carries social cost | Improves only via borrowed credibility and adjacency, never via direct assertion (§5) |
| Under-35 share decline is partly **a share-of-category artefact** (fewer buyers in the category at that age, later household formation) | Nothing to fix — and we should say so rather than spend against it |

Two of these seven would materially change the recommendation. One of them would tell us to stop.

### 2.2 The diagnostic we propose

Eight weeks, no design freeze until it reports. **Cost $640K.**

1. **Distinctive-asset audit** — unprompted recall and *correct attribution* of every element we currently protect, tested separately in the base and in 18–34. Assets are kept or retired on measured attribution, not on internal affection (§4).
2. **Cohort decomposition** — is under-35 decline a penetration, frequency, or category-participation effect? Panel data, not survey opinion.
3. **Availability audit** in the channels the cohort uses, including marketplace share-of-search and quick-commerce presence.
4. **Rejection interviews** — 40 conversations with under-35 *category buyers who considered and declined us*, plus 15 with under-35 buyers who chose us (the most under-studied group in the file).
5. **Base sensitivity work** — 20 depth conversations with long-tenured buyers on what, specifically, felt like betrayal last time. Our hypothesis, offered to be corrected: it was not the aesthetics. It was being made the punchline.
6. **Post-mortem** of the two previous campaigns using their own tracking data, read for the *shape* of the failure rather than for blame.

This is the cheapest consequential decision in the programme.

### 2.3 The uncomfortable question, answered rather than deferred

**What if the answer is that this brand cannot recruit under-35s at acceptable cost?**

It is a legitimate outcome. If the diagnostic shows the occasion is structurally in decline and entry-price economics cannot be met, then the correct strategy is *not* a repositioning: it is a disciplined harvest of a highly profitable loyal franchise, with growth capital redirected to acquisition or to an adjacent house brand. We would rather name that possibility now, in a paper recommending investment, than discover it in Year 3.

**We therefore propose that §7 Gate 1 include an explicit "harvest and redeploy" option**, with the same standing as "proceed". If the sponsor group is unwilling to entertain that option, the diagnostic becomes theatre and we would suggest not funding it.

---

## 3. What is fixed: four brand invariants, stated as floors

Framed as what the brand owes, not as how any execution must look — so that very different work can honour them.

### 3.1 Invariant I — the promise does not move
**Floor:** the functional promise the brand has made for seventy years is restated, not replaced. Repositioning changes *who we say it to and how*; it does not change what we said. If the promise itself is wrong, this is not a repositioning and needs a different paper.

### 3.2 Invariant II — the two or three genuinely distinctive assets survive, and remain recognisable at a glance
**Floor:** any asset with measured unaided attribution above the threshold set in §4.2 must remain identifiable **from across a shop floor, by an existing customer, without reading**. Craft may be modernised freely. Recognition may not be interrupted. The most expensive error available to us is the loss of instant findability by the people who already buy.

### 3.3 Invariant III — every claim is demonstrable
**Floor:** nothing is said about the brand that cannot be shown. Heritage is used only in the form of *evidence* — the same process, the same specification, the same place, the receipts — never in the form of sentiment. Nostalgia is a message to the base and reads as decay to everyone else.

### 3.4 Invariant IV — the tone floor: the brand is never the joke, and never mocks its own past
**Floor:** no execution positions the brand's previous era, or the people who loved it, as something the brand has grown out of. Self-aware humour is permitted and encouraged; self-*deprecating* humour that implicates the base is prohibited. This is the invariant most often broken by good agencies working at speed, and the one that caused the last backlash.

### 3.5 Everything else is renewable property
Format, size, price ladder, sub-brand naming, packaging craft, typography beneath the recognition threshold, casting, register, channel mix, partners, music, pace, and the internal name of this programme.

### 3.6 The alternative-form process (in place of exemption)
A market, account or line that cannot honour a floor is not asked to refuse. It is asked to **propose the nearest form it can honour**, on two pages: which floor, why, the alternative, and the condition under which the floor becomes reachable. Approver: **CMO, countersigned by the squad lead and by Legal/Regulatory where a claim is involved.** Twelve months, renewable once with fresh reasoning. Logged in an internally published register, reviewed at each phase gate. An alternative form is accepted unless materially weaker than the floor. **We expect three to six in Year 1 and would be suspicious of zero.**

---

## 4. Preserve, evolve, retire — decided by measurement, not by affection

### 4.1 The sorting rule

Two questions, in this order: *does it carry recognition?* and *does it carry the meaning we want?* The combination, not either alone, decides.

| | **Carries the meaning we want** | **Carries meaning we do not want** |
|---|---|---|
| **High recognition** | **Preserve, modernise craft only.** Wordmark core, colour, the shape/format signature, the quality cue | **Evolve slowly and under cover.** Retire the *meaning* while keeping the *mark* — usually via context and usage, not redesign. Never in one step |
| **Low recognition** | **Free to renew.** Secondary palette, typography below threshold, illustration style, layout system | **Retire quietly.** No announcement, no explanation, no farewell |

### 4.2 The threshold we propose
An asset qualifies as protected at **≥45% correct unaided attribution among category buyers**, or **≥60% among the loyal base**. Below both figures it is a preference, not an asset, and should be treated as freely renewable regardless of how long it has been in the guidelines.

### 4.3 Our working hypotheses (to be replaced by §2.2 data)

| Element | Disposition | Reasoning |
|---|---|---|
| Wordmark, core colour, format/shape signature | **Preserve.** Redraw for digital legibility at 24px; do not restructure | These are the entire asset base. Interrupting them saves nothing and costs everything |
| Founding date / "Since 19xx" lockup | **Preserve, but re-employ.** Move from front-of-pack sentiment to proof-of-standard context | The date is not the problem; using it as an emotional appeal is |
| Heritage crest / ornamental period devices | **Evolve, slowly** — simplify across a staggered pack rollout, one sub-range at a time over 18 months | High recognition, wrong meaning. A single-step change here is what "modernisation" looked like last time |
| Legacy tagline | **Retire quietly** at natural media expiry; do not replace with a new tagline in Year 1 | A new tagline is a claim. We have not yet earned one |
| Long-standing spokesperson / mascot / voice, if present | **Preserve and give it better material.** Do not retire an asset the base uses to find us | Retiring a beloved figure is read as a verdict on the people who loved it |
| Period photography style, ornate copy register, legacy sub-brand names with no attribution | **Free to renew** | Nobody is holding on to these but us |
| The previous modernisation campaign's assets | **Retire fully and without commentary** | Any reference reopens the wound and invites the comparison |

### 4.4 The rule that governs all of the above
**Never subtract in public.** Every change is introduced as an *addition* — a new line, a new format, an additional occasion — and legacy elements are retired later, quietly, once the addition has established itself. Additions are welcomed; removals are grieved. The same net change produces two entirely different reactions depending on which of these it is made to look like.

---

## 5. Positioning, channel and content

### 5.1 The positioning, in the form we would use internally

> **For seventy years this has been made to one standard. That has not changed. What we make it into is changing, because what people need it for has changed.**

Note what this does not do. It does not claim youth. It does not apologise. It does not ask the base to accept a new identity — it tells them the standard they bought into is being defended. And it gives an under-35 buyer the only thing the brand can offer that a new competitor cannot: **verifiable consistency in a category full of brands three years old**.

### 5.2 Relevance is earned in this order, and the order is the strategy

| Step | What moves | What we say publicly |
|---|---|---|
| 1. **Fit** | Format, size, price entry point, occasion | Nothing about the brand. Only about the thing |
| 2. **Findability** | Marketplace, quick-commerce, share-of-search, discovery retail | Nothing |
| 3. **Proof** | Craft transparency — the factory, the specification, the people, the seventy-year receipts | Show, do not characterise |
| 4. **Borrowed credibility** | Mid-tail creators and small partners who already use the brand, or plausibly could | Their words, not ours |
| 5. **Participation** | Community, limited runs, co-creation, archive access | Invite, do not announce |
| 6. **Assertion** | Master-brand expression at scale | Only now, and only using language the audience gave us in steps 3–5 |

We would ask the sponsor group to note that **steps 1–3 have almost no advertising content**, and that the previous two attempts both began at step 6.

### 5.3 Channel approach

| Channel | Role | Y1 posture |
|---|---|---|
| **Retail media & marketplace search** | Availability and conversion where the cohort actually buys. Unglamorous, and the highest-yield line in the plan | ~30% of working budget |
| **Mid-tail creators (10k–250k)** | Borrowed credibility; volume of independent voices beats one large voice. Long-term retainers over one-off posts; brief on the *invariants*, never on the words | ~25%. Hard rule: no creator is asked to say the brand has changed |
| **Owned community & CRM (two tracks)** | The base track and the entrant track are **separate lists, separate content, separate cadence**. The base hears everything first | ~10% |
| **Craft/provenance content (long and short form)** | Proof at scale; the single most transferable asset a 70-year-old brand has | ~15% |
| **Trade & retailer partnership** | Shelf, listings for new formats, and pre-emption of buyer anxiety | ~10% |
| **Broad-reach paid brand media** | Deliberately underweight in Y1; scales in Y2 once we know what to say | ~10%, rising to ~35% in Y2 |
| **Earned/PR** | Reactive only in Y1. No repositioning story is offered to press | — |

### 5.4 The mockery pre-mortem (mandatory gate on every asset)

Before any asset

# Global Employee Empowerment & Adaptive Culture Initiative
## Guidance on Regional Leadership Adaptation — Recommendation for Sponsor Group

**Version 2.0 — complete. Prepared for sponsor group decision, and for prior circulation to the fourteen regional people leads. Not yet for employee communication.**

---

### How we would ask you to use this

One note only, and then the substance.

This version differs from v1.0 in three ways that the reviewers were right to insist on. It now asks for specific decisions, with money and a date attached (§12). It answers the questions the first draft deferred — most importantly what the centre itself is bound by (§9). And the regional material has been re-cut so that no colleague opens it and finds their country described inside someone else's card.

The regional cards in §6 remain what they were: **working hypotheses, offered so that they can be corrected**. Where a region has its own diagnostic data, that data replaces the card and the card is retired for that unit (§5.4). A card returned to us unamended will be read not as agreement but as a sign that the conversation has not yet taken place, and we would come back for it.

Two courtesies we would ask the sponsor group to extend before this travels further. First, that the fourteen regional people leads and the four regional MDs see §§3, 4 and 9 and have time to respond in their own way before the board pack is assembled — a programme about devolved authority that arrives in a region fully formed has already contradicted itself, and colleagues will notice that before they notice anything else. Second, that §10 (consultation and legal gates) be walked through with Group Legal, the European Works Council secretariat and Group Reward before any part of this is described to employees anywhere. The likeliest single cause of avoidable damage is a well-intentioned announcement that reaches a works council after it reaches a newspaper, or reaches an employee before it reaches their own supervisor.

---

## 1. Recommendation on a page

**Adopt a thin global core and a wide local expression: four employee entitlements defined centrally as *floors*, with a formal alternative-form process where a floor cannot lawfully or structurally be met; delivery method, language, sequencing and naming devolved entirely to regions; four instrumented pilots in Year 1 with a common measurement spine but deliberately different local design; and a published protocol binding the centre to the same discipline it asks of others.**

| | |
|---|---|
| Global mandate | **Four entitlements only** (§3) — decision rights at the lowest competent level; an answered route for dissent; tolerance of good-faith error; employee-initiated internal movement. Each stated as a floor, each with a named-approver alternative-form route (§3.6) |
| Devolved to regions | Language, ritual, sequencing, symbolism, manager incentives, pace, communication channels, and the programme's name. We would suggest the centre resist standardising even the name |
| Year 1 shape | **Four pilots — one high-authority-distance, one low, one deskless-majority, one recently-acquired entity** — different in design, identical in instrumentation (§7) |
| Principal risk | Middle-manager status and grade loss, not employee resistance (§8) |
| The centre's own obligation | **Published reversal protocol**: the centre may reverse a devolved decision, but must give written reasons to the same audience that saw the decision, and reversal counts are reported quarterly beside regional metrics (§9) |
| Measurement | Within-region trend on four behavioural proxies weighted 70%, survey items 30%; acquiescence correction applied before any cross-region view is shown (§8.3) |
| Numeric failure test | Empowerment survey index +5 points or more while decision latency on the instrumented decision class improves <10% and internal-move rate is flat = declared failure, programme paused, no further capital (§8.5) |
| Investment sought | **$14.2M Year 1, $10.6M Year 2** (illustrative, assumptions in §12.1), of which $6.9M is manager time relief — the line most often omitted and most often fatal |
| Funding split | Central P&L funds diagnostic, instrumentation, platform, central team and pilot facilitation; regions fund manager time with a **60% central offset in Y1, 30% in Y2, nil thereafter** (§12.3) |
| Decisions requested | **Three** — §12.5, sought at the sponsor group meeting on **18 March** |
| Programme owner | Group Chief People Officer, sponsor; named programme director recruited internally within 30 days of approval |

### 1.1 The core proposition, and how confident we are in it

Empowerment mechanisms do not transfer between contexts; the conditions that make them work can be built in each. *(This is our considered assertion from practitioner experience, not a finding — see the evidence key at §14. We flag it because the sponsor group is entitled to know which of our statements are evidenced and which are judgement.)*

The specific failure we are trying to avoid is well documented in our own past programmes: exported behavioural vocabulary — "speak up", "own it", "disagree and commit" — produces regions that become fluent at the annual survey and unchanged on Tuesday morning. That outcome is worse than no initiative, because it consumes the credibility a second attempt would require.

---

## 2. Diagnosis before we design

### 2.1 The framing we would gently ask the sponsor group to test

The initiative is currently described as culture change. The evidence available to us may instead describe a **decision-rights and information-flow** problem wearing culture-change clothing. Only one of those two responds to leadership behaviour work, and we would rather establish which we have before committing eight figures to the wrong one.

| Candidate driver | What leadership/empowerment training does to it |
|---|---|
| Decision rights formally held too high | Nothing — requires delegation-of-authority redesign |
| Rights delegated on paper, retracted in practice | Nothing until retraction is made visible and costly (§9) |
| Information does not reach the level holding authority | **Amplifies harm** — confident decisions on poor data |
| Managers lack coaching capability | Improves, *if* paired with funded time relief (§8.4) |
| Reward and grading pay for control, not for developing others | Nothing — the incentive wins every time (§8.2) |
| Employees have voice but no evidence it is ever acted on | Worsens — a further unanswered invitation deepens cynicism |
| Working-language barrier suppresses contribution | Nothing — needs channel design, not confidence-building (§11.1) |

### 2.2 The diagnostic we propose

Five weeks, no design freeze until it reports: 60 structured conversations across four organisational levels in eight countries (including two deskless-majority sites); an audit of the documented delegation-of-authority matrix against actual practice in twelve units; and a language-barrier check in the four sites where the working language is not the local one. Cost **$310K**.

If it finds that decision rights are formally too high, the largest part of the Year 2 training envelope should be redirected to delegation architecture and the pilot scope revised before commitment. This is the cheapest consequential decision in the programme.

### 2.3 The uncomfortable question, now answered rather than deferred

Will headquarters be bound by the same four entitlements? If regional colleagues discover that the centre reserves the right to overturn devolved decisions without giving reasons, the initiative becomes rhetoric and everything downstream of it is wasted. v1.0 left this open. **§9 now answers it with a specific, testable, reportable mechanism**, and we would ask the sponsor group to adopt or amend it rather than to note it.

---

## 3. What is fixed everywhere: four entitlements, stated as floors

Framed as what an employee is entitled to, not as how a manager must behave, so that very different conduct can honour them.

### 3.1 Entitlement I — decision rights sit at the lowest competent level
**Floor:** every employee can name the classes of decision they own and point to a recent instance of exercising one without seeking permission. *Competent* is doing real work in that sentence; this is not an argument for uniform flat structures.

### 3.2 Entitlement II — there is a route for dissent, and it is answered
**Floor:** every employee has at least one available channel through which they can contradict a superior's view **and receive a response**. The channel may be a written pre-read, a skip-level, a facilitated small group, a mentor, a shift huddle, or an anonymous board. It need never be a raised hand in a large meeting. The answered part is the floor; the form is entirely local.

**Firewall, mandatory:** this channel is expressly **not** a statutory reporting channel. Disagreement about a business decision is not a protected disclosure. The two must be separately named, separately routed and separately governed, or we create legal exposure on one side and chill genuine reporting on the other (§10.3).

### 3.3 Entitlement III — good-faith error is absorbed, not attributed
**Floor:** within each unit, at least one specific, visible instance per quarter in which a good-faith mistake was absorbed rather than attributed, and the team can name it. Demonstrated, never announced. In several regions this must be framed collectively rather than individually to be usable at all (§6).

### 3.4 Entitlement IV — employees can initiate their own movement
**Floor (revised from v1.0):** an employee may apply for an internal role, project or rotation **without the incumbent manager holding a veto and without the manager being informed in advance of the application**.

v1.0 stated this as an absolute and was wrong to. In parts of the Gulf, mobility between entities is constrained by employer-tied work permits and is a legal matter, not a cultural one. In Japan, Korea and Taiwan, seniority-anchored career and reward structures make unrestricted lateral self-nomination structurally disruptive in ways that a global mandate cannot responsibly overrule from a distance. The floor above is the most we can hold everywhere; where even that cannot be met, §3.6 applies.

### 3.5 Everything else is regional property
Language, ceremony, sequencing, symbolism, tooling, incentives, cadence, and the programme's own name.

### 3.6 The alternative-form process (in place of exemption)

We deliberately avoid the word *exemption*, and avoid asking any region to refuse. A region that cannot meet a floor is asked instead to **propose the nearest form it can honour**, and to say what it would take to close the remainder.

| Element | Provision |
|---|---|
| Trigger | Legal impossibility, collective-agreement conflict, or structural impossibility (not difficulty, not discomfort) |
| Form | Two pages: which floor, why, the alternative mechanism proposed, and the condition under which the floor becomes reachable |
| Approver | **Group Chief People Officer**, countersigned by the Regional MD and by Group Legal |
| Duration | **12 months maximum**, renewable once with fresh reasoning |
| Visibility | Entered in an internally published register, reviewed quarterly by the sponsor group |
| Presumption | An alternative form is accepted unless it is materially weaker than the floor. We expect four to eight across the network in Year 1 and would be suspicious of zero |

---

## 4. The adaptation logic

### 4.1 Four variables, rather than a general culture model

We would ask each region to place itself on four axes only, because these four determine whether a given mechanism functions or backfires.

| Axis | The question | What it changes |
|---|---|---|
| **Authority basis** | Does a manager's authority derive from role or from demonstrated expertise? | Whether devolution reads as trust or as abandonment |
| **Directness of disagreement** | Can dissent be public without cost to either party? | The design of the dissent channel (Entitlement II) |
| **Attribution of error** | Does a mistake attach to a person, a team, or a system? | Whether error tolerance can be individual or must be collective (III) |
| **Ambiguity tolerance** | Is an open brief experienced as freedom, or as information withheld? | How much structure must accompany autonomy |

### 4.2 The working rule

> High authority distance and low disagreement-directness do not mean empowerment is unwelcome. They mean it must be **granted rather than seized** — granted visibly, specifically, bounded, and by someone whose authority the team already accepts.

In such contexts an open invitation ("bring me your ideas") is not empowerment; it is a test most colleagues will decline to sit. The functioning equivalent is a named, bounded, publicly conferred mandate: *"Priya decides this class of exception up to this threshold. She does not need to ask me. If you disagree with her, take it to her."* Our practitioner judgement is that this single act moves more behaviour than a quarter of workshops — offered as judgement, not as measured finding (§14), and testable inside the pilots via the decision-latency proxy.

### 4.3 Sponsorship: a default with a visible opt-out

**Default:** regional sponsors are selected on observed practice — leaders whose own teams already exhibit the four entitlements — rather than on rank.

We acknowledged in v1.0 that this backfires in several regions, then handed the choice back, which was no recommendation at all. The corrected position: the default stands, and a region wishing to depart from it does so through a **one-page note countersigned by the Regional MD and the programme director**, logged in the same register as §3.6. Departures are expected and unremarkable; what matters is that they are visible.

Where the practitioner sponsor sits two or three levels below the Regional MD, the workable form is almost always a **pair** — the senior figure as visible patron providing cover and air, the practitioner as the working engine. A junior sponsor without a senior patron will in several regions be read, reasonably, as the centre not taking the region seriously.

---

## 5. Using the regional cards well

### 5.1 What they are
Starting hypotheses about context, to be returned marked up within 45 days. They describe patterns we have observed in workplaces, not peoples.

### 5.2 What each card contains

**Younger consumers do not reject old brands. They reject brands that perform youth.** Age is not the liability; *pretending* is. The problem is currently described as a brand-perception problem. The available evidence may instead describe a **format, occasion and availability** problem wearing brand-perception clothing. | Candidate driver of under-35 decline | What a repositioning campaign does to it |
|---|---|
| The product is right but the **format/pack size** does not fit under-35 households, spaces or occasions | Nothing — needs range work |
| The brand is absent from the **channels where the cohort actually shops** (marketplace, quick-commerce, discovery-led retail) | Nothing — needs distribution work; awareness without availability is a tax |

### 4.1 The sorting rule

Two questions, in this order: *does it carry recognition?* and *does it carry the meaning we want?* The combination, not either alone, decides.

| | **Carries the meaning we want** | **Carries meaning we do not want** |
|---|---|---|

An asset qualifies as protected at **≥45% correct unaided attribution among category buyers**, or **≥60% among the loyal base**. Below both figures it is a preference, not an asset, and should be treated as freely renewable regardless of how long it has been in the guidelines.

| The previous modernisation campaign's assets | **Retire fully and without commentary** | Any reference reopens the wound and invites the comparison |

### 4.4 The rule that governs all of the above
**Never subtract in public.** Every change is introduced as an *addition* — a new line, a new format, an additional occasion — and legacy elements are retired later, quietly, once the addition has established itself. Additions are welcomed; removals are grieved. The same net change produces two entirely different reactions depending on which of these it is made to look like.

### 5.1 The positioning, in the form we would use internally

> **For seventy years this has been made to one standard. That has not changed. What we make it into is changing, because what people need it for has changed.**

### 1.1 The core proposition, and how confident we are in it

**Younger consumers do not reject old brands. They reject brands that perform youth.** Age is not the liability; *pretending* is. ## 2. Diagnosis before we design

### 2.1 The framing we would gently ask the sponsor group to test

The problem is currently described as a brand-perception problem. The available evidence may instead describe a **format, occasion and availability** problem wearing brand-perception clothing. Only one of those responds to repositioning work, and we would rather know which we have before committing eight figures to the wrong one.

| Candidate driver of under-35 decline | What a repositioning campaign does to it |
|---|---|
| The product is right but the **format/pack size** does not fit under-35 households, spaces or occasions | Nothing — needs range work |
| The brand is absent from the **channels where the cohort actually shops** (marketplace, quick-commerce, discovery-led retail) | Nothing — needs distribution work; awareness without availability is a tax |
| **Price-per-unit architecture** blocks trial at the entry point | Nothing — the entry price wins every time |
| The **occasion the brand serves has itself declined**, independent of brand age | Actively harmful — repositions into a shrinking room |
| The cohort has **no problem with the brand and no reason to think about it** | Improves, *if* paired with proof and availability |
| The cohort **actively codes the brand as their parents'** and that coding carries social cost | Improves only via borrowed credibility and adjacency, never via direct assertion (§5) |

Eight weeks, no design freeze until it reports. **Cost $640K.**

1. **Distinctive-asset audit** — unprompted recall and *correct attribution* of every element we currently protect, tested separately in the base and in 18–34. Assets are kept or retired on measured attribution, not on internal affection (§4).
2. **Cohort decomposition** — is under-35 decline a penetration, frequency, or category-participation effect? Panel data, not survey opinion.
3. **Availability audit** in the channels the cohort uses, including marketplace share-of-search and quick-commerce presence.

5. **Base sensitivity work** — 20 depth conversations with long-tenured buyers on what, specifically, felt like betrayal last time. Our hypothesis, offered to be corrected: it was not the aesthetics. It was being made the punchline.
6. **Post-mortem** of the two previous campaigns using their own tracking data, read for the *shape* of the failure rather than for blame.

This is the cheapest consequential decision in the programme.

**What if the answer is that this brand cannot recruit under-35s at acceptable cost?**

It is a legitimate outcome. We would rather name that possibility now, in a paper recommending investment, than discover it in Year 3.

## 3. What is fixed: four brand invariants, stated as floors

Framed as what the brand owes, not as how any execution must look — so that very different work can honour them.

### 3.1 Invariant I — the promise does not move
**Floor:** the functional promise the brand has made for seventy years is restated, not replaced. Repositioning changes *who we say it to and how*; it does not change what we said. If the promise itself is wrong, this is not a repositioning and needs a different paper.

### 3.2 Invariant II — the two or three genuinely distinctive assets survive, and remain recognisable at a glance
**Floor:** any asset with measured unaided attribution above the threshold set in §4.2 must remain identifiable **from across a shop floor, by an existing customer, without reading**. Craft may be modernised freely. Recognition may not be interrupted. The most expensive error available to us is the loss of instant findability by the people who already buy.

### 3.3 Invariant III — every claim is demonstrable
**Floor:** nothing is said about the brand that cannot be shown. Heritage is used only in the form of *evidence* — the same process, the same specification, the same place, the receipts — never in the form of sentiment. Nostalgia is a message to the base and reads as decay to everyone else.

### 3.4 Invariant IV — the tone floor: the brand is never the joke, and never mocks its own past
**Floor:** no execution positions the brand's previous era, or the people who loved it, as something the brand has grown out of. Self-aware humour is permitted and encouraged; self-*deprecating* humour that implicates the base is prohibited. This is the invariant most often broken by good agencies working at speed, and the one that caused the last backlash.

Format, size, price ladder, sub-brand naming, packaging craft, typography beneath the recognition threshold, casting, register, channel mix, partners, music, pace, and the internal name of this programme.

## 4. Preserve, evolve, retire — decided by measurement, not by affection

### 4.1 The sorting rule

Two questions, in this order: *does it carry recognition?* and *does it carry the meaning we want?* The combination, not either alone, decides.

| | **Carries the meaning we want** | **Carries meaning we do not want** |
|---|---|---|
| **High recognition** | **Preserve, modernise craft only.** Wordmark core, colour, the shape/format signature, the quality cue | **Evolve slowly and under cover.** Retire the *meaning* while keeping the *mark* — usually via context and usage, not redesign. Never in one step |
| **Low recognition** | **Free to renew.** Secondary palette, typography below threshold, illustration style, layout system | **Retire quietly.** No announcement, no explanation, no farewell |

### 4.2 The threshold we propose
An asset qualifies as protected at **≥45% correct unaided attribution among category buyers**, or **≥60% among the loyal base**. Below both figures it is a preference, not an asset, and should be treated as freely renewable regardless of how long it has been in the guidelines.

### 4.3 Our working hypotheses (to be replaced by §2.2 data)

| Element | Disposition | Reasoning |

| Wordmark, core colour, format/shape signature | **Preserve.** Redraw for digital legibility at 24px; do not restructure | These are the entire asset base. Interrupting them saves nothing and costs everything |

| Heritage crest / ornamental period devices | **Evolve, slowly** — simplify across a staggered pack rollout, one sub-range at a time over 18 months | High recognition, wrong meaning. A single-step change here is what "modernisation" looked like last time |

| Long-standing spokesperson / mascot / voice, if present | **Preserve and give it better material.** Do not retire an asset the base uses to find us | Retiring a beloved figure is read as a verdict on the people who loved it |
| Period photography style, ornate copy register, legacy sub-brand names with no attribution | **Free to renew** | Nobody is holding on to these but us |
| The previous modernisation campaign's assets | **Retire fully and without commentary** | Any reference reopens the wound and invites the comparison |

### 4.4 The rule that governs all of the above
**Never subtract in public.** Every change is introduced as an *addition* — a new line, a new format, an additional occasion — and legacy elements are retired later, quietly, once the addition has established itself. Additions are welcomed; removals are grieved. The same net change produces two entirely different reactions depending on which of these it is made to look like.

Earn relevance through product, format, price entry and availability *before* claiming it in communication. Carry the new formats on an endorsed sub-brand so that risk is contained. ### 1.1 The proposition, and how confident we are in it

**Younger consumers do not reject old brands. They reject brands that perform youth.** Age is not the liability; pretending is. A seventy-year-old brand can make one claim no new entrant can buy — that it has done this, the same way, for seventy years, and can show you the receipts — and the previous two campaigns traded that asset for borrowed contemporary signalling the brand had not earned.

*This is practitioner judgement, not a finding. See the evidence key at §12. The sponsor group is entitled to know which of our statements are evidenced and which are ours.*

### 1.2 A correction to something v1.0 asserted too strongly

Version 1.0 said base trust is "effectively non-recoverable". The brief's own record contradicts that: the previous campaigns "briefly alienated" the base and the base returned. The honest statement is narrower and, we think, more useful:

> Base trust has proved recoverable twice, at a cost in credibility we have not measured. What we cannot evidence is that it is recoverable a third time. Each incident teaches long-tenured customers that the brand is capable of disowning them, and that lesson compounds. We are therefore treating base trust as a **depleting reserve with an unknown balance** — which argues for the same caution as irrecoverability, but for a reason we can defend.
